```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, echo = FALSE,
                      fig.retina = 3, fig.align = "center",
                      dev = "ragg_png")  # ragg finds Fira Sans Condensed on Windows
```

```{r packages-data, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
source(here::here("R", "slide-things.R"))

# Colors from the slide theme, all readable on white ----
clr_bar <- "#538ba2"
clr_soft <- "#c5d9e2"
clr_mean <- "#a93e31"
clr_median <- "#244a70"
clr_mode <- "#8a6100"

theme_slides <- function(base_size = 20) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
    theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
          axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1)))
}

fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)

# Baseline and endline math scores ----
baseline <- read_csv(here::here("files", "data", "mindspark", "ms_blel_jpal_baseline.csv"),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
endline <- read_csv(here::here("files", "data", "mindspark", "ms_blel_jpal_endline.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE)
math <- baseline$tot_math
n_all <- length(math)
n_end <- nrow(endline)
n_treat <- sum(baseline$treat == 1)
n_control <- sum(baseline$treat == 0)

# Frequency table, with every score from lowest to highest ----
score_f <- tibble(score = math) %>%
  count(score, name = "f") %>%
  complete(score = min(math):max(math), fill = list(f = 0)) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * f / n_all)
score_top <- score_f$score[which.max(score_f$f)]
f_top <- max(score_f$f)
zero_scores <- score_f$score[score_f$f == 0]

# Grouped table, with intervals of 5 ----
group_table <- function(x) {
  tibble(score = x) %>%
    mutate(low = 5 * floor(score / 5)) %>%
    count(low, name = "f") %>%
    complete(low = seq(0, 25, 5), fill = list(f = 0)) %>%
    mutate(interval = paste0(low, "–", low + 4), mid = low + 2)
}
grouped <- group_table(math)
top_interval <- grouped$interval[which.max(grouped$f)]

# Twenty real students for the exercise ----
set.seed(2)
try_scores <- sample(math, 20)
try_table <- group_table(try_scores) %>% filter(low <= 15)
try_top <- try_table$interval[which.max(try_table$f)]

# Girls and boys, for the percentages ----
n_girls <- sum(baseline$st_female1 == 1)
n_boys <- sum(baseline$st_female1 == 0)
by_group <- baseline %>%
  mutate(group = if_else(st_female1 == 1, "Girls", "Boys"),
         low = 5 * floor(tot_math / 5)) %>%
  count(group, low, name = "f") %>%
  complete(group, low = seq(0, 25, 5), fill = list(f = 0)) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  mutate(pct = 100 * f / sum(f)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(mid = low + 2)

# Students per center ----
centers <- baseline %>%
  count(ms_center1, name = "f") %>%
  mutate(ms_center1 = fct_reorder(ms_center1, -f))

# First rows of the data ----
first_rows <- baseline %>%
  slice(1:6) %>%
  transmute(Student = st_id, Center = ms_center1, Grade = st_grade1, Female = st_female1,
            Treatment = treat, Hindi = tot_hindi, Math = tot_math)
```

# Recap: The Mindspark study

.box-1.small.sp-after-half[Does the Mindspark program improve children's learning?]

.pull-left-3[

After-school centers in Delhi, India

Software that adapts to each child, plus small-group help from a teaching assistant
]

A quick recap from Tuesday. We'll use this study all quarter, so every new method gets tried on these same children.

Each session was about 45 minutes on the software and 45 minutes with a teaching assistant.

# Frequency tables

---

layout: true
class: title title-6

# A frequency table counts each score

.pull-left[
.box-inv-6.small[Left column: each score X]

.box-inv-6.small[Right column: how many students, called the frequency f]

.box-6.small[Show every category, even a zero]
]

.pull-right[
```{r frequency-rules, results="asis"}
score_f %>%
  filter(score >= 20) %>%
  transmute(`Score X` = score, f = f) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "c", table.attr = 'class="deck-table tight"')
```

.center.small[Nobody scored `r paste(zero_scores, collapse = " or ")`]
]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

A gap in the table would hide something real: nobody scored 22. The next slide has the full table.

These are whole-number scores. The test could give anything from 0 to 35, and the highest anyone scored was `r max(math)`.

The book lists the highest score at the top. Either order is fine.

---

# The full table has a peak at `r score_top`

```{r frequency-full, results="asis"}
full_table <- score_f %>%
  mutate(f = if_else(score == score_top, paste0('<strong class="peak">', f, "</strong>"), as.character(f)),
         score = if_else(score == score_top, paste0('<strong class="peak">', score, "</strong>"), as.character(score)))
per_col <- ceiling(nrow(full_table) / 3)
bind_cols(full_table[1:per_col, c("score", "f")],
          full_table[(per_col + 1):(2 * per_col), c("score", "f")],
          full_table[(2 * per_col + 1):(3 * per_col), c("score", "f")],
          .name_repair = "minimal") %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "c", escape = FALSE, col.names = rep(c("Score X", "f"), 3),
        table.attr = 'class="deck-table tight tighter"')
```

.box-inv-6.small[The f column adds up to n = `r sum(score_f$f)`, so every student is counted once]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019). In the book, this total is written N.]

---

# Grouping trades detail for clarity

.pull-left[
.box-inv-6.small[Ten or fewer intervals is typical]

.box-inv-6.small[Use a simple width: 2, 5, 10 or 20]

.box-inv-6.small[Start at a multiple of the width]

.box-inv-6.small[Keep all intervals the same width]
]

.pull-right[
```{r frequency-grouped, results="asis"}
grouped %>%
  transmute(`Interval` = interval, f = f) %>%
  kable(format = "html", align = "c", table.attr = 'class="deck-table tight"')
```
]

.box-6.small[Inside `r top_interval`, we no longer know any one student's exact score]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

These are guidelines, so use good judgment. With a width of 5 we get six intervals, down from `r nrow(score_f)` rows.

---

class: center middle section-title section-title-3 animated fadeIn

# Plots and shapes

---

layout: true
class: title title-3

---

# A histogram draws the grouped table

```{r histogram, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.3, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("Histogram of baseline math scores in intervals of 5, with touching bars labeled with their counts: ", paste0(grouped$interval, " has ", grouped$f, collapse = ", "), ". The tallest bar is ", top_interval, ".")}
ggplot(grouped, aes(x = mid, y = f)) +
  geom_col(width = 5, fill = clr_bar, color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = f), vjust = -0.4, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", color = clr_median,
            family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = grouped$mid, labels = grouped$interval) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline (out of 35)", y = "Students (f)") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[Each bar is one row of the table. The bars touch: the scale has no gaps]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# A polygon swaps bars for dots and lines

```{r polygon-grouped, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.3, out.width="84%", fig.alt="The same histogram in pale blue, with a dark line on top. Each dot sits at the middle of an interval at the height of its bar, and the line drops to zero at both ends. The line rises to a peak at the interval from 10 to 14 and then falls."}
poly_grouped <- bind_rows(tibble(mid = -3, f = 0), select(grouped, mid, f), tibble(mid = 32, f = 0))

ggplot(grouped, aes(x = mid, y = f)) +
  geom_col(width = 5, fill = clr_soft, color = "white") +
  geom_line(data = poly_grouped, color = clr_median, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = poly_grouped, color = clr_median, size = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = grouped$mid, labels = grouped$interval) +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline (out of 35)", y = "Students (f)") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[Each dot sits at the middle of its interval. A line is easier to overlay than bars]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

The line drops to zero one interval past each end, so the shape closes on the axis.

---

# Every score: more detail, more bumps

```{r polygon-full, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.3, out.width="84%", fig.alt=paste0("A polygon with one dot for every score from 0 to ", max(math), ". It rises to a jagged peak of ", f_top, " students at a score of ", score_top, ", with a sharp dip right after it, and then falls to almost nothing above 20.")}
poly_full <- bind_rows(tibble(score = min(math) - 1, f = 0), score_f, tibble(score = max(math) + 1, f = 0))

ggplot(poly_full, aes(x = score, y = f)) +
  geom_line(color = clr_median, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(color = clr_median, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = score_top + 1, y = f_top, label = paste(f_top, "students scored", score_top),
           hjust = 0, color = clr_median, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, max(math), 2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.08))) +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline (out of 35)", y = "Students (f)") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[With no grouping we keep every count, and the picture gets jagged]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

---

# Percentages put groups on one scale

```{r percentages, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.9, out.width="90%", fig.alt=paste0("Two polygons of baseline math scores for ", n_girls, " girls and ", n_boys, " boys. In the left panel, which shows counts, the line for girls towers over the line for boys. In the right panel, which shows the percent of each group, the two lines have nearly the same height and shape.")}
panels <- by_group %>%
  pivot_longer(c(f, pct), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("f", "pct"),
                        labels = c("Number of students (f)", "% of each group")))
group_labels <- tibble(scale = factor("Number of students (f)", levels = levels(panels$scale)),
                       mid = c(14, 19.5), value = c(max(by_group$f), 68), group = c("Girls", "Boys"),
                       text = c(paste0("Girls, n = ", n_girls), paste0("Boys, n = ", n_boys)))

ggplot(panels, aes(x = mid, y = value, color = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = group_labels, aes(label = text), hjust = 0, size = 6, fontface = "bold",
            family = "Fira Sans Condensed", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Girls = clr_median, Boys = clr_mean), guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Girls = "solid", Boys = "dashed"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = grouped$mid, labels = grouped$interval) +
  facet_wrap(vars(scale), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline", y = NULL) +
  theme_slides(18)
```

.box-inv-3.small[% = 100 × f / n. On the left, size hides the shape. On the right, we can compare]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

The shapes are the point. Girls and boys look much alike once we use percentages. There are simply about `r round(n_girls / n_boys)` times as many girls in this sample.

---

# A density plot smooths out the bumps

```{r density, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.9, out.width="80%", fig.alt="The percentage of students at each math score, shown as pale bars, with a smooth dark curve running through them. The curve has one peak near 12 and falls away evenly on both sides."}
ggplot(baseline, aes(x = tot_math)) +
  geom_col(data = score_f, aes(x = score, y = pct), fill = clr_soft, width = 0.85) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density) * 100), color = clr_median, linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 16.5, y = 9.5, label = "Kernel density plot", hjust = 0, color = clr_median,
           size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 26, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Math score at baseline (out of 35)", y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[It adds up a small bump at each score. You'll read these, not compute them]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

The name is fancy, the idea isn't. Smooth curves are how we'll draw distributions for the rest of the quarter, starting with the normal curve.

---

# Categories get bars with gaps

```{r bar-graph, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.7, out.width="80%", fig.alt=paste0("Bar graph of students at the three Mindspark centers, with gaps between the bars: ", paste0(centers$ms_center1, " has ", centers$f, collapse = ", "), ".")}
ggplot(centers, aes(x = ms_center1, y = f)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, fill = clr_bar) +
  geom_text(aes(label = f), vjust = -0.4, size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", color = clr_median,
            family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(x = "Mindspark center", y = "Students (f)") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-3.small[Scores have an order and even steps, so a histogram's bars touch. Centers are just names, so these bars stand apart]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

This is Tuesday's scales of measurement at work. Nominal and ordinal variables get a bar graph. Interval and ratio variables get a histogram or polygon.

---

# Symmetric, unimodal and normal differ

```{r shapes, fig.width=11, fig.height=2.9, out.width="92%", fig.alt="Three curves side by side. The first has two equal peaks and mirrors around its center, so it's symmetric but not unimodal. The second has one peak on the left and a long tail to the right, so it's unimodal but not symmetric. The third is a bell curve: symmetric, unimodal and normal."}
shape_grid <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 300)
shapes <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = shape_grid, y = 0.5 * dnorm(shape_grid, 3, 0.9) + 0.5 * dnorm(shape_grid, 7, 0.9),
         shape = "Symmetric, not unimodal"),
  tibble(x = shape_grid, y = dgamma(shape_grid, 3, 1), shape = "Unimodal, not symmetric"),
  tibble(x = shape_grid, y = dnorm(shape_grid, 5, 1.4), shape = "Normal: both, and a bell")
) %>%
  mutate(shape = fct_inorder(shape))

ggplot(shapes, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_area(fill = clr_soft, color = clr_bar, linewidth = 1.1) +
  facet_wrap(vars(shape), nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slides(18) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

.pull-left-3[
.box-inv-3.small[Symmetric: each side mirrors the other]
]

.pull-middle-3[
.box-inv-3.small[Unimodal: one high point]
]

.pull-right-3[
.box-inv-3.small[Normal: a bell, common in nature]
]

???

A normal distribution is symmetric and unimodal, with the most scores in the middle. Not every symmetric, unimodal shape is normal, but that's a detail for later.

Our math scores are unimodal and close to symmetric. Many measurements in nature look like this, which is why the bell curve keeps coming back.

---

# Skewed distributions have one long tail

```{r skew, fig.width=11, fig.height=3.1, out.width="90%", fig.alt="Two curves. On the left, a peak near the high end with a long tail stretching to the left, labeled skewed left. On the right, a peak near the low end with a long tail stretching to the right, labeled skewed right."}
skews <- bind_rows(
  tibble(x = shape_grid, y = dgamma(10 - shape_grid, 3, 1), shape = "Skewed left"),
  tibble(x = shape_grid, y = dgamma(shape_grid, 3, 1), shape = "Skewed right")
)
tails <- tibble(shape = c("Skewed left", "Skewed right"), x = c(1.9, 8.1), y = c(0.07, 0.07),
                label = c("Long tail", "Long tail"))

ggplot(skews, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_area(fill = clr_soft, color = clr_bar, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_text(data = tails, aes(label = label), color = clr_median, size = 6, fontface = "bold",
            family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(shape), nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_slides(18) +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

.pull-left[
.box-inv-3.small[A very easy test: scores pile up high, and a few trail off to the left]
]

.pull-right[
.box-inv-3.small[A very hard test: scores pile up low, and a few trail off to the right]
]

.book-tag[In the book: skewed left is negatively skewed, and skewed right is positively skewed]

???

Skew is named after the tail, not the peak. That's the common mistake. Tuesday we'll see what a long tail does to the mean.

---

layout: false
class: title title-8

# Predict it: The endline scores

.box-inv-8.small.sp-after-half[The same study, about 4.5 months later. Picture the baseline curve you just saw. What does the endline curve look like?]

.options[
.option[
**A** In about the same place
]
.option[
**B** Moved right, still one peak
]
.option[
**C** Moved right, now two peaks
]
.option[
**D** Moved left
]
]

.box-8.small[Tell a neighbor why. Half these students had Mindspark, and half didn't]

???

About 6 minutes. Hands are fine here. Ask a few students to defend their answer before the next slide, especially anyone who picked C. If half got a program and half didn't, why wouldn't we see two peaks?

---

class: title title-8

# Predict it: The whole pile moved right

```{r endline, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.8, out.width="82%", fig.alt=paste0("Two smooth curves of math scores, on a percent scale. The baseline curve, for ", n_all, " students, peaks near 12. The endline curve, for ", n_end, " students, sits about 6 points to the right. It's wider and lower, with one broad peak.")}
rounds <- bind_rows(tibble(score = math, round = "Baseline"),
                    tibble(score = endline$tot_math, round = "Endline"))

ggplot(rounds, aes(x = score, color = round, linetype = round)) +
  geom_density(aes(y = after_stat(density) * 100), linewidth = 1.5, bw = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 5.3, y = 9.2, label = paste0("Baseline, n = ", n_all), hjust = 1, color = clr_median,
           size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  annotate("text", x = 24.5, y = 6.5, label = paste0("Endline, n = ", n_end), hjust = 0, color = clr_mean,
           size = 6.5, fontface = "bold", family = "Fira Sans Condensed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Baseline = clr_median, Endline = clr_mean), guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(Baseline = "solid", Endline = "dashed"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 35, 5)) +
  labs(x = "Math score", y = "% of students") +
  theme_slides()
```

.box-inv-8.small[So, B: one wide peak. Half the students scored at least `r median(math)` at baseline, and half at least `r median(endline$tot_math)` at endline]

.source[Data: Muralidharan, Singh, and Ganimian (2019).]

???

Percentages again, because the two rounds have different numbers of students.

Why not two peaks, with one group ahead? At endline the treatment group's mean is about `r round(mean(endline$tot_math[endline$treat == 1]) - mean(endline$tot_math[endline$treat == 0]), 1)` points higher, but scores spread much wider than that, so the two piles overlap into one.

Why did the pile move? Everyone had 4.5 more months of school, and half also had Mindspark. A plot of everyone can't separate those two. That's what the rest of the course is for: this is description, and explanation comes later.

The endline tests aren't identical to the baseline test. They were out of 34 or 35, depending on the grade band. So treat this as a rough picture.
